title: The many faces of Wiraqucha
description: From Incan transcription to Unicode: why Wiraqucha is more than a domain name.

body:
# The many faces of Wiraqucha

No important name has only one face. **Wiraqucha** appears as a ​figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in turn: the ‌name and its roots, the Incan transcription original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in a browser. ‌Taken together, those faces explain why *viracocha* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Wiraqucha
- **ASCII ​form:** viracocha
- **Meaning:** "Sea of fat"
- **Domain of influence:** Creator, Sky, Sea Foam
- **Pantheon:** Incan
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form

## Overview

**Wiraqucha** (*viracocha*) — Creator, Sky, Sea Foam · Sea of fat — belongs to the ​Incan tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Creator, Sky, Sea Foam". The name means "Sea of fat".

**Wiraqucha** is creator, sky, sea foam. The name means "Sea of fat" and belongs ​to the incan tradition.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Wiraqucha** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/viracocha/). The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose. No indigenous written attestation ​survives for this name; **Wiraqucha** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "Sea of fat".

The ASCII form *viracocha* survives only because the early domain-name system could ‌not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The form **Wiraqucha** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes ​the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

## Mythology

The stories of Wiraqucha place ​creator, sky, sea foam at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Wiraqucha appears in incan tradition as creator, sky, sea foam. The name's meaning, "Sea of fat", shapes the narratives ​told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Wiraqucha in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Wiraqucha survive ​in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations ​so that readers can compare them. The restoration Wiraqucha gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### The Flood of Unu Pachakuti (Betanzos ch. 1)

Juan de Betanzos, whose *Suma y ​Narración de los Incas* (1551) is the fullest early account, tells that Wiraqucha made the first people at Tiwanaku and gave them the world to keep; but they grew proud and lived without ‌worship, so he resolved to undo them. He sent a great flood — *unu pachakuti*, a watery overturning of the world — that drowned the first race, the wari, while he himself rose ​into the sky above Titicaca. Yet he spared two, a man and a woman, calling them from the waters onto a float of totora reeds near the island, and commissioning them as the ‌ancestors of a new humanity. The myth fixes the shape of Andean time: catastrophe and renewal in cycles, a world unmade and remade, with the creator always watching from above. It is also ​a charter for the lake itself — Titicaca is not scenery but the hinge where the first world ended and the second began.

### The Making of Nations at Tiwanaku (Cobo 13.3)

Father Bernabé ‌Cobo's *Historia del Nuevo Mundo* (Book 13) preserves the imperial version: after the flood, Wiraqucha set to work at Tiwanaku, where he sculpted the forms of all the nations to come — each ​with its own face, dress, language, songs, and seeds — and brought them to life. When the work was done he dispatched them, calling them out of caves, springs, and rivers to find ‌their homelands: one nation he sent by way of a cave, another along a river's course, and to the Inca ancestors he gave the special charge that would lead them at last to Cusco. ​Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa's *Historia Indica* (ch. 6–7) gives the same program and adds the full titulature: Ticci Uiracocha Pachayachachic, 'ancient foundation, creator of the world.' The myth is a map of the ‌Andes read backward — every people is the deliberate work of the same hand, and the Inca are simply the nation that remembered best who made them.

### The Sun, Moon, and Stars (Sarmiento ​ch. 7)

The same accounts make Wiraqucha the maker of the sky. On the island of Titicaca in the great lake he fashioned the Sun — Inti — and the Moon, and set ​the stars in their courses, appointing the Sun the most honored of all, 'like a rich ornament' among the rest (Sarmiento de Gamboa, ch. 7; Cobo 13.3). In imperial theology Inti then became ‌the visible ancestor of the Inca dynasties, while Wiraqucha remained the invisible maker behind the visible god — a two-tier heaven in which the sun was, as it were, the son, and the ‌emperor the sun's line. The pairing let Cusco worship a present, national god without ever forgetting the older, unbounded one above and behind him. It is one of the few world mythologies in ‌which the supreme creator deliberately steps back from the machinery of daily rule, delegating the visible sky to his own workmanship and reserving for himself only the authorship of everything.

## Symbols & Iconography

​The iconography associated with Wiraqucha concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Wiraqucha, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Creator, ​Sky, Sea Foam

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Wiraqucha across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a claim ‌about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Wiraqucha carries the same precision in textual form.

- **Sea foam of the lake** — The etymon wira-qucha, 'foam (or fat) of the lake' — the ​foam from which the name, and the god, emerged
- **The staff and traveler's bundle** — He crossed the Andes as a staff-carrying beggar, weeping at springs and prophesying — the god as itinerant ​stranger
- **The reed float** — The totora-reed float that bore the two survivors of the flood — the seed of the remade world
- **The stone models of Tiwanaku** — The sculpted prototypes of ‌every nation, from which Wiraqucha shaped humankind at his workshop
- **The golden image of Cusco** — The solid-gold statue in the Coricancha, described by Cobo and Murúa and melted down within years of ​the conquest

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Wiraqucha with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Incan name of ​this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable ‌forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming Wiraqucha, sanctuary or cult remains tied to creator and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the ​name before entering the scholarly record.

## A Meditation

To contemplate Wiraqucha is to hold the idea of creator, Sky, Sea Foam in the mind and to ask what of it endures. The name means "Sea of fat" ​— and a name that carries its meaning so openly invites meditation rather than mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as creator, Sky, Sea Foam · Sea of fat.

Sit with the ‌restored form — Wiraqucha — and the diacritics themselves become the practice: each mark is a small act of attention, a refusal to let the plain ASCII form *viracocha* stand in for the ​whole. What the tradition preserved in this name, the restoration asks the reader to preserve in turn.

## A Closer Look at ‌the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Wiraqucha**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Incan ​transcription rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *viracocha* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public ​reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project ​prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **v**, **i**, **r**, **a**, **c**, **o**, **c**, **h**, **a** ‌— so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and ​addressable.

## Wiraqucha in Its Tradition

**Wiraqucha** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Incan tradition, where it is counted among 11 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Creator, Sky, Sea ‌Foam — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company ​of its kin. When the address bar shows **Wiraqucha**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point ‌of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Wiraqucha** is one such ​vote.

## The Restoration on the Live Web

A domain name is a kind of publication. When **Wiraqucha** resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is not a theoretical ​exercise; it is a working address on the public internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, and anyone who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. ​That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. Before Unicode domains, a scholar could write the name correctly in an article while the public web flattened it to *viracocha*. Now the public ‌web can carry the correct form end to end. The punycode translation happens silently, so the infrastructure remains compatible while the visible name keeps its marks. That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding ‌— is the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.
